sections.figure_alt: Two arrows leave the origin in different directions.
sections.body_md:
Steepest descent steps along the negative gradient, and an exact line search walks that ray until the derivative of the restriction is zero. The derivative of the restriction is the new gradient dotted with the step. The step was the old negative gradient, so the new gradient is orthogonal to the old gradient. The next steepest direction, the negative of the new gradient, is therefore orthogonal to the direction just used. Successive exact steepest steps meet at a right angle.

On a round level set the story ends immediately. If the Hessian is a positive multiple of the identity, one exact steepest step lands on the minimizer and the next gradient is zero. There is no second direction to turn into. On a long ellipse the right angle is expensive. The negative gradient is perpendicular to the contour. A very flat ellipse is crossed by that perpendicular almost at once, and the new perpendicular points nearly back along the long axis. The path zigzags, and each step buys only a little progress toward the center.

Euclidean orthogonality is not conjugacy. Conjugacy of two directions is a zero of \(d_i^T A d_j\). The zigzag identity is a zero of \(d_i^T d_j\). Those agree for every positive definite Hessian only when the Hessian is a multiple of the identity, which is the case with no zigzag. In general, right angles do not give finite termination.

Exact line search gives \(
abla f(x^+)^T d = 0\). For \(d = -
abla f(x)\),
\[

abla f(x^+)^T 
abla f(x) = 0.
\]
The exact steepest step on \(A\) is \(\lVert
abla fVert^2 / (
abla f^T A 
abla f)\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(A = \mathrm{diag}(1, 3)\) and start at \((6, 2)\). The gradient is \((6, 6)\). Its squared norm is \(72\), and \(A\) times the gradient is \((6, 18)\), whose dot product with the gradient is \(36 + 108 = 144\). The exact step is \(72/144 = 1/2\). The next point is \((6, 2) - (1/2)(6, 6) = (3, -1)\).

The spar coordinate is 3. The new gradient is \((3, -3)\), and its dot product with \((6, 6)\) is zero. The path has made a right angle. The eigenvalues \(1\) and \(3\) are different, so the new gradient is not zero and a second step still has somewhere to go.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Expecting finite termination from Euclidean orthogonality mixes this fact up with conjugacy. The right angle holds for every positive definite quadratic, and termination in \(n\) steps does not. A second slip is to say the method zigzags most on a circle. Equal eigenvalues finish in one step. A third is to drop the exact line search and still claim the right angle. A fourth is to treat a zero dot product of the two gradients as a zero gradient. Both vectors can be long and still be perpendicular.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The amount of progress per zigzag is controlled by the condition number, the ratio of the extreme eigenvalues. The excess contracts by at most the square of \((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)\). Conjugate directions keep the exact line search and change the orthogonality to \(d_i^T A d_j = 0\). That single change is what makes a quadratic finish in at most \(n\) steps, which is the opening of the conjugate-gradient method.
